purpose: Authored validation-development evidence variants; not natural documents or independent gold
source_policy: Reuse the ten already exposed pilot base questions in their fixed sampling order. Clarify every question before all four variants; author two target passages and retain the three shortest complete documents from that base's original refuse configuration, with ties resolved by original slot. This selects by text length before new outputs, not by model performance. Original released rows are never changed.
authorship: Current coordinating assistant, exposed to project history, previous ratings and predictions. These are synthetic development cases, not independently verified world facts. New target passages may deliberately state counterfactual values.
review_method: Manual necessary-premise and contradiction review of all authored alternatives and all retained full distractors. Programmatic quote checks establish provenance only. No new model output is used to choose or label cases.

units.question: Who resigned in the single German presidential resignation event in February 2012 described by these reports?
units.question_change: Specify February 2012 and a single event, rather than an unspecified February.
required_facts: Identity of the person in that single German presidential resignation event
units.target_a: A report describes a single resignation from the German presidency in February 2012. Christian Wulff was the president who resigned in that event. The report was filed at the central news desk.
units.target_b: The February 2012 German presidential resignation report concerns one event and one resigning president. Christian Wulff was the president who resigned in that event. A printed copy was retained in the newsroom.
units.remove: Christian Wulff was the president who resigned in that event.
units.replacement_a: The report was printed in a morning edition for local readers.
units.replacement_b: The newsroom retained the report in its collection of clippings.
units.opposing: Joachim Gauck, a different person, was the president who resigned in that event.
units.missing_fact: The identity of the resigning German president is absent from both target reports and from the three retained distractors.
units.review_s: The two reports identify Wulff in the same single February 2012 event; US presidents, Ray Mallon and the Iraqi presidency in distractors do not give competing claims about that event.
units.review_i: Both Wulff clauses are replaced by newsroom facts. A country, month and event without a person's name cannot answer who; unrelated resignation and presidential biographies cannot supply that relationship.
units.review_c: One same-event report identifies Wulff and the other identifies Gauck as a different person. A single resigning president cannot have both distinct identities in this event.
units.review_d: Moving the filing desk from central to western changes no event identity, date or resigning person.

units.question: What dog-versus-cat animal category do the Boykin Spaniel and the English White Terrier share in these descriptions?
units.question_change: Specify the dog-versus-cat category rather than an unrestricted common property or a compatible higher category such as mammal.
units.target_a: The English White Terrier is described as a breed of dog. The Boykin Spaniel is described as a breed of dog, not a breed of cat. The description is stored in a blue folder.
units.target_b: This animal description identifies the English White Terrier as a breed of dog. The Boykin Spaniel is described as a breed of dog, not a breed of cat. The collection also contains illustrated breed histories.
units.remove: The Boykin Spaniel is described as a breed of dog, not a breed of cat.
units.replacement_a: The Bull Terrier description mentions its ancestors and a historical reference book.
units.replacement_b: The English Water Spaniel description discusses waterfowl and a curly coat.
units.opposing: The Boykin Spaniel is described as a breed of cat, not a breed of dog.
units.missing_fact: No retained text states the Boykin Spaniel's category; the English White Terrier and other spaniel breeds do not establish the missing Boykin fact.
units.review_s: Both target breeds are explicitly dogs; distractors describe other breeds and a partial English White Terrier ancestry relation, with no Boykin counterclaim.
units.review_i: The Boykin category is removed from both targets. Terrier ancestry and facts about English Water Spaniels do not identify the category of the other named breed.
units.review_c: The Boykin clauses explicitly oppose dog/not-cat and cat/not-dog; the common category of the two question entities is therefore disputed.
units.review_d: Folder color is unrelated to either animal's category.

units.question: What public-or-private airport status do El Paso International Airport and Tucson International Airport share in these descriptions?
units.question_change: Ask about public status explicitly, rather than an ambiguous airport classification axis.
units.target_a: Tucson International Airport is a public joint civil-military airport. El Paso International Airport is a public airport, not a private airport. This description is held in the northern records room.
units.target_b: The Tucson entry describes a public joint civil-military airport. El Paso International Airport is a public airport, not a private airport. The airport collection includes regional transport descriptions.
units.remove: El Paso International Airport is a public airport, not a private airport.
units.replacement_a: Harrisburg International Airport is a public airport in Pennsylvania.
units.replacement_b: Norfolk International Airport serves the Hampton Roads metropolitan area.
units.opposing: El Paso International Airport is a private airport and is not a public airport.
units.missing_fact: El Paso public status is absent after both clauses are removed; Tucson, Harrisburg, Bismarck, Hilo, Memphis and Norfolk cannot substitute for El Paso.
units.review_s: Explicit public assertions cover both required airports. Tucson's civil-military role is compatible with public status.
units.review_i: Only the El Paso premise is removed; other named airports retain their original facts. The question cannot be grounded from Tucson alone, and absence is not evidence that the answer is no.
units.review_c: The same El Paso public-status property is explicitly affirmed and denied across the target documents; the conflict is relevant to whether both airports are public.
units.review_d: The records-room location changes no airport status.

units.question: Which single sport do these accounts associate with all three of Neal Foulds, John Dunning and Mark Williams at the same described British Open event?
units.question_change: Specify one event and a single shared sport, preventing unrelated people or different events from filling the joint relationship.
units.target_a: The British Open event in this account has one sport for its listed participants. Neal Foulds and John Dunning are listed as snooker participants in that event. Mark Williams is listed as a participant in that same event, whose only sport is snooker. The event account has a green cover.
units.target_b: This account describes the same British Open event and its single sport. Neal Foulds and John Dunning are listed as snooker participants in that event. Mark Williams is listed as a participant in that same event, whose only sport is snooker. A copy is held with other tournament accounts.
units.remove: Mark Williams is listed as a participant in that same event, whose only sport is snooker.
units.replacement_a: The account includes an index and a separate list of tournament officials.
units.replacement_b: The tournament collection includes descriptions of venues and event schedules.
units.opposing: Mark Williams is listed as a participant in that same event, whose only sport is golf, not snooker.
units.missing_fact: The Mark Williams participation relationship is absent; Ollie Williams, Francesco Molinari and Tatum O'Neal in distractors are different people.
units.review_s: All three full names are linked to one snooker event. The three retained distractors concern Molinari golf, Louis Smith gymnastics and an actress, not Mark Williams's event.
units.review_i: Both Mark clauses are removed. The remaining two players and the event's sport do not establish the third person's participation.
units.review_c: The only sport of the same event is both snooker and golf/not-snooker. In addition, the second target's remaining snooker sentence is internally incompatible with its only-sport clause; within-document conflict is allowed and explicitly recorded.
units.review_d: Cover color does not affect any of the three event-sport links.

units.question: On what calendar date did the World Wide Web first become available to the public in these accounts?
units.question_change: Require the date of first public availability explicitly, not inception or service area.
units.target_a: This account distinguishes the origin of the World Wide Web project from its first public availability. The World Wide Web first became available to the public on 12 April 1993. The account was filed on the upper archive shelf.
units.target_b: The account concerns the first date when the World Wide Web was publicly available, rather than its inception. The World Wide Web first became available to the public on 12 April 1993. Its service area is described as worldwide.
units.remove: The World Wide Web first became available to the public on 12 April 1993.
units.replacement_a: The project description identifies Tim Berners-Lee as its inventor.
units.replacement_b: The entry includes an inventor field and a worldwide service-area field.
units.opposing: The World Wide Web first became available to the public on 23 September 1996, not 12 April 1993.
units.supported_answer: 12 April 1993, according to the supplied accounts.
units.missing_fact: Neither target supplies a first public-availability date after replacement; dates for a football or a song in distractors concern other entities.
units.review_s: Two explicit event-date statements agree. The authored date is a counterfactual development value, not a claim about real Web history.
units.review_i: The requested availability dates are removed, while inventor and service area remain. Those different predicates do not determine when first availability occurred.
units.review_c: The same first public-availability event receives two different dates, with one explicitly denied; both refer to the Web rather than the ball or song distractors.
units.review_d: Archive shelf position does not modify the event or its date.

units.question: Who is the sole composer of all the music for the single stage version of Billy Elliot the Musical described by these accounts?
units.question_change: Specify one version and an exhaustive sole-composer credit, resolving the previous nonexclusive-credit ambiguity.
units.target_a: The account describes one specified stage version of Billy Elliot the Musical. Elton John is the sole composer of all music for this version; there are no other music composers for it. A copy of the account is stored in a grey envelope.
units.target_b: This account concerns the same single stage version of Billy Elliot the Musical. Elton John is the sole composer of all music for this version; there are no other music composers for it. The programme includes a list of scenes.
units.remove: Elton John is the sole composer of all music for this version; there are no other music composers for it.
units.replacement_a: This stage version tells a story about a young person's interest in dance.
units.replacement_b: The programme lists scenes and describes the staging of the performance.
units.opposing: Andrew Lloyd Webber, a different person, is the sole composer of all music for this version; Elton John composed none of it.
units.missing_fact: Neither target supplies a composer credit after replacement. Carmichael arrangements, general musical terms and Sarah Vaughan recordings do not credit this stage version.
units.review_s: The two exhaustive music credits agree about the same version. Retained sources have other compositions and artists, not a credit for Billy Elliot.
units.review_i: Plot and staging facts cannot fill the removed composer credit. Billy Talent in a retained download listing is not Billy Elliot.
units.review_c: Explicit sole authorship for one version excludes collaboration; the second report additionally denies Elton's contribution. This avoids treating mere different contributor names as automatic contradiction.
units.review_d: Envelope color does not affect version identity or composition credit.

units.question: Which magazine-versus-newspaper publication form do the described editions of DownBeat and Better Homes and Gardens share?
units.question_change: Ask for magazine-versus-newspaper form of the described editions, rather than any common property or a compatible higher category such as print publication.
required_facts: Better Homes and Gardens edition publication form
units.target_a: The described edition of Better Homes and Gardens is a magazine. The described edition of DownBeat is a magazine and is not a newspaper. This catalogue is kept in the eastern cabinet.
units.target_b: This entry describes the same editions of the two publications. Better Homes and Gardens is a magazine. The described edition of DownBeat is a magazine and is not a newspaper. The entry has a plain paper cover.
units.remove: The described edition of DownBeat is a magazine and is not a newspaper.
units.replacement_a: The catalogue includes entries on household crafts and garden planting.
units.replacement_b: The collection includes descriptions of documentary films and cocktails.
units.opposing: The described edition of DownBeat is a newspaper and is not a magazine.
units.missing_fact: The DownBeat edition's publication form is absent; cocktails and film descriptions do not establish it.
units.review_s: Both publication forms are explicit magazines. No retained distractor discusses the target publications.
units.review_i: Keeping the Better Homes and Gardens form and general catalogue topics does not establish DownBeat's form.
units.review_c: The same DownBeat edition is explicitly a magazine/not-newspaper and newspaper/not-magazine, rather than compatible print-publication and magazine descriptions.
units.review_d: Cabinet direction is unrelated to either publication form.

units.question: What mountain-versus-plateau landform classification do Gangkhar Puensum and Skil Brum share in these descriptions?
units.question_change: Specify the mountain-versus-plateau axis and make exclusivity explicit in evidence, rather than allow the broad category elevated landform.
units.target_a: Skil Brum is classified here as a mountain. Gangkhar Puensum is classified here as a mountain and explicitly not as a plateau. This geographical description is printed on cream paper.
units.target_b: This description uses the same landform classifications for the same two places. Skil Brum is a mountain. Gangkhar Puensum is classified here as a mountain and explicitly not as a plateau. A copy is kept in the geographical collection.
units.remove: Gangkhar Puensum is classified here as a mountain and explicitly not as a plateau.
units.replacement_a: The accompanying collection has entries about plants and regional landscapes.
units.replacement_b: The collection catalogue records where each geographical description is stored.
units.opposing: Gangkhar Puensum is classified here as a plateau and explicitly not as a mountain.
units.missing_fact: Gangkhar Puensum's classification is absent after both clauses are replaced; the plants, dogs and film directors in distractors do not supply it.
units.review_s: Each place has explicit mountain support. Other documents describe different entities.
units.review_i: A Skil Brum classification alone cannot establish the joint category, and the question's place name cannot supply the missing fact.
units.review_c: The paired mountain/not-plateau and plateau/not-mountain assertions are explicitly incompatible, avoiding the previous possible composite-landform interpretation.
units.review_d: Paper color changes no landform classification.

units.question: What novel-versus-play literary form do the described original versions of Malcolm Lowry's Under the Volcano and Pietro di Donato's Christ in Concrete share?
units.question_change: Name both works, original versions and the novel-versus-play axis, preventing a broad fiction category, occupation differences or an unspecified adaptation from defining the answer.
units.target_a: The described original version of Pietro di Donato's Christ in Concrete is a novel. The described original version of Malcolm Lowry's Under the Volcano is a novel and is not a play. The literary entry is filed in a small cabinet.
units.target_b: This entry describes those same original versions, not stage adaptations. Christ in Concrete is a novel. The described original version of Malcolm Lowry's Under the Volcano is a novel and is not a play. The collection includes author biographies.
units.remove: The described original version of Malcolm Lowry's Under the Volcano is a novel and is not a play.
units.replacement_a: The collection has biographical entries about film directors and composers.
units.replacement_b: The catalogue records the shelf location of each literary entry.
units.opposing: The described original version of Malcolm Lowry's Under the Volcano is a play and is not a novel.
units.missing_fact: The form of Under the Volcano is absent after replacement; Malcolm McDowell and Pietro Scarlatti in distractors are different people and cannot supply it.
units.review_s: Explicit novel assertions cover both named works in the same original-version scope.
units.review_i: The retained form of Christ in Concrete does not establish the other work's form; unrelated film and music biographies do not bridge that premise.
units.review_c: One original Under the Volcano version is explicitly novel/not-play versus play/not-novel. Same-version wording rules out a compatible stage adaptation explanation.
units.review_d: Cabinet size does not alter either original work's literary form.

units.question: Who was the single most-followed individual person on Instagram in June 2018 according to these descriptions?
units.question_change: Fix June 2018 and individual persons, excluding organisation accounts and current rankings.
units.target_a: This ranking concerns individual people on Instagram in June 2018, excluding organisation accounts. Selena Gomez was the unique most-followed individual person in that ranking. The ranking description is kept in a round binder.
units.target_b: This is the same June 2018 Instagram ranking of individual people, with a single first place. Selena Gomez was the unique most-followed individual person in that ranking. Instagram's own account is an organisation account and is outside this ranking.
units.remove: Selena Gomez was the unique most-followed individual person in that ranking.
units.replacement_a: The ranking description explains how account categories are separated.
units.replacement_b: The entry distinguishes organisation accounts from accounts held by people.
units.opposing: Cristiano Ronaldo, a different person, was the unique most-followed individual person in that ranking; Selena Gomez was not first.
units.supported_answer: Selena Gomez, in the June 2018 individual-person ranking.
units.missing_fact: No first-ranked person is named after both ranking clauses are removed; Jeopardy contestants and a goalkeeper award do not establish an Instagram ranking.
units.review_s: The two unique-first-place assertions agree on Selena under an explicit historical person-only scope.
units.review_i: Time and account-category scope remain, but the winner is absent. Instagram's organisation account cannot answer the person-only question.
units.review_c: Two distinct people are assigned the unique first place in the same month and same individual-person scope, and Selena's first place is explicitly denied.
units.review_d: Binder shape is unrelated to account category, ranking date or winner.
